newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin office says Juppe misled French on deficit.
newsitem.headline: Jospin office says Juppe misled French on deficit.

text.p: Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's office said on Friday that a leaked note by ex-prime minister Alain Juppe showed the defeated centre-right government had misled the French people on the extent of the public deficit.
The note, given by the conservative ex-premier to his Socialist successor at their handover on June 4, was published by Reuters and the French media on Thursday.

It showed that revenue would fall 35 billion francs ($5.9 billion) short of the amount in the 1997 published budget and forecast that France's public deficit would swell to 4.0 percent of gross domestic product next year, far above the three percent target set by the Maastricht treaty for a single European currency.

"This note has to be checked because it is in total, absolute contradiction with their campaign speeches which told us that the deficits were well on their way to being reduced," Jospin's spokesman, Manuel Valls, told reporters.
He said it proved that the independent audit ordered by Jospin for July 21 was essential to get a true picture.
"Either they knew the situation, in which case they lied, or they didn't know it, and thus the audit becomes even more necessary," Valls said.

Juppe's note acknowledged that additional austerity measures would be needed this year to bring down the deficit to meet the Maastricht treaty criteria, something he consistently denied during the parliamentary election campaign in April and May.
New conservative Gaullist opposition leader Philippe Seguin seized on the publication of the leaked memorandum to argue that the audit was unnecessary and just a delaying tactic by Jospin.

But Valls replied: "Contrary to what is said here and there, this work is not only useful but indispensable, since we don't know what the exact situation is, and each number behind the decimal point is important."
"We are not going to fiddle the figures. This is 'operation truth' on the figures," he added.

Other government sources said they expect the audit to show the 1997 deficit is running at between 3.5 and 3.7 percent of GDP, and that Jospin would announce measures as soon as it is issued to reduce this year's shortfall.

But Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has said publicly that France will not make the strict "three-point-zero" definition of the budget criterion demanded by hardliners in Germany and the target should be interpreted as a trend, as the treaty allows.
The sources say the government aims to present a 1998 draft budget in September which respects the three percent criterion, thus showing that the trend is in the right direction.

However they acknowledged that that will be difficult since the government will not have the once-off benefit of a 37 billion franc cash injection it received this year from taking over state-owned France Telecom's pension fund and liabilities.

Valls said that once the government had the true figures, it would take the necessary measures to meet France's European commitments, while taking account of Jospin's priorities of boosting growth, encouraging job-creation and reducing social injustice.
"There will be no austerity plan," he said. Strauss-Kahn has indicated the government is weighing extra taxes on corporate profits, well-off households and savings. ($ = 5.926 French Francs)
